problem: The text says a solution exists "only when" every pair agrees, which reads as one-directional. The condition aᵢ ≡ aⱼ (mod gcd(mᵢ,mⱼ)) for all pairs is also sufficient: it is exactly the test for existence.
fix: Write: "A solution exists if and only if aᵢ ≡ aⱼ (mod gcd(mᵢ,mⱼ)) for every pair i, j. When this holds, the solution is unique modulo lcm(m₁,…,mₖ); when it fails, there is no solution at all."

problem: The moduli are never restricted to integers greater than 1. If any mᵢ = 1 the notion of pairwise coprime (and the inverse Mᵢ⁻¹ mod mᵢ in Section 2) breaks down, because there is no inverse modulo 1.
fix: State at the start: "Each modulus mᵢ is a positive integer with mᵢ > 1." Add to the construction: "Each mᵢ must be greater than 1, so that a residue and an inverse modulo mᵢ are defined."

problem: "to solve systems of congruences in coding and cryptography" repeats the general idea instead of naming a use, so it tells the student nothing concrete.
fix: Replace with a concrete use, for example: "to reconstruct a number from its residues in fast computer arithmetic, and to build threshold secret-sharing schemes."

problem: The speed argument compares only the size of the two small exponentiations with one large one, and does not mention that the receiver performs two of them plus a recombination step. A student can lose track of the total cost.
fix: Add: "The receiver does two exponentiations of about half the bit length instead of one of full length. Each costs roughly a quarter of the full one, so the total, plus the CRT recombination, is about half the work."
